headline_marked: Microsoft AI's MAI-Transcribe-2 [[undercuts OpenAI, Google, ElevenLabs]] on price and speed
headline: Microsoft AI's MAI-Transcribe-2 undercuts OpenAI, Google, ElevenLabs on price and speed
summary: Microsoft AI's new speech-recognition model is 72% cheaper than its predecessor and boasts faster, more accurate results across 60 languages.
details: Microsoft AI has launched MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model that claims to outperform OpenAI, Google, and ElevenLabs in speed, accuracy, and cost. The model is priced at an aggressive 10 cents per hour of audio, a significant reduction from its previous $0.36 per hour rate.

This new release is part of Microsoft's strategy to build its own frontier-class AI models across various modalities, aiming to reduce reliance on partners like OpenAI. MAI-Transcribe-2 represents a major step in this direction, showcasing the company's capability in developing competitive AI solutions.

The model supports 60 languages, an expansion from the 43 supported by its predecessor, MAI-Transcribe-1.5. It is designed to handle real-world audio challenges such as background noise and overlapping speech, making it suitable for enterprise applications like call center analysis.

Key features include speaker diarization to identify different speakers, word-level timestamps for precise timing, and keyword biasing to improve accuracy with domain-specific jargon. It also offers automatic language identification, eliminating the need for manual language selection.

MAI-Transcribe-2 provides a configurable output style, with a 'verbatim' mode preserving all speech elements for compliance purposes and a 'clean' mode for more readable transcripts. It also handles 'code switching,' seamlessly transcribing conversations that shift between languages.

Microsoft claims MAI-Transcribe-2 ranks first on the FLEURS benchmark for multilingual speech recognition with a 5.2% word error rate across 60 languages. It also ranks second on the Artificial Analysis leaderboard for accuracy and latency, indicating strong real-world performance.

headline_marked: [[ICE Buys $2M Spyware]] That Hacks Phones Without a Click
headline: ICE Buys $2M Spyware That Hacks Phones Without a Click
summary: Paragon's Graphite spyware can infiltrate smartphones and steal data from encrypted apps like WhatsApp and Signal without any user interaction.
details: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has awarded a $2 million contract to Paragon Solutions for its 'Graphite' spyware. This sophisticated tool is capable of compromising smartphones without requiring the user to click a link or download anything, raising significant privacy concerns.

Graphite operates similarly to NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, falling into the category of 'mercenary spyware' developed and sold to government agencies. While both offer covert access to targeted phones, Graphite is reportedly designed to primarily extract data from messaging applications.

The spyware can access information from apps like WhatsApp and Signal, even with end-to-end encryption enabled. It achieves this by exploiting vulnerabilities in how phones process incoming messages and files before they are displayed, allowing it to run commands and install itself silently.

Researchers have confirmed Graphite's ability to perform 'zero-click' attacks, exploiting flaws in message inspection processes. This means infections can occur without any user error or awareness, making detection extremely difficult.

In late 2024, Citizen Lab helped WhatsApp identify and block an active Graphite exploit. Approximately 90 users, including journalists and activists, were warned in January 2025 that their accounts had been targeted by Paragon's spyware.

Forensic evidence confirmed Graphite infections on the phones of Italian immigration activists and journalists. Italian prosecutors later provided independent confirmation of spyware traces on these devices, dating back to December 2024.

The spyware has also been confirmed to target Apple devices, exploiting a previously unknown iMessage vulnerability that Apple has since patched in iOS 18.3.1. This marks the first forensic confirmation of Graphite compromising an iPhone.

While Italian agencies confirmed using Graphite for legally authorized surveillance related to immigration and national security, conflicting accounts exist regarding the company's and officials' involvement in specific cases.
